concepts.name: Thread-local values in coroutines with asContextElement
kotlinx.serialization: unknown keys and coerced values
Full-text search in Room with FTS tables

questions.prompt: A logging library reads the request ID from a `ThreadLocal`. You set it at the start of a coroutine on `Dispatchers.IO`, but after a suspending call the logs show a wrong ID. What fixes it?

choices.text: Run the coroutine on `Dispatchers.Unconfined`, so it never changes thread
Set the value once in `Application.onCreate()`, so every thread shares it
Add `requestId.asContextElement(id)`, which restores it on every resume
Read it with `coroutineContext[ThreadLocal]`, which follows the coroutine

questions.explanation: A coroutine can resume on a different pool thread after any suspension, and a `ThreadLocal` belongs to a thread. `asContextElement(value)` adds a context element that puts the value back every time the coroutine switches context. `Unconfined` doesn't help: after the first suspension it resumes on whatever thread the suspending function used.

sources.title: Coroutine context and dispatchers
sources.claim: `ThreadLocal.asContextElement` keeps a value and restores it every time the coroutine switches its context; a value set inside the coroutine is not propagated and is lost on the next suspension (use `withContext` to change it); `Dispatchers.Unconfined` resumes on whatever thread the suspending function used.

questions.prompt: The backend adds a new `badge` field to the feed JSON. The released app decodes with a default `Json` instance and now fails on every response. Which setting prevents this?

choices.text: `coerceInputValues = true`, so any unexpected input is replaced by defaults
`isLenient = true`, so the parser accepts input that isn't strict JSON
`explicitNulls = false`, so keys missing from the class decode as null
`ignoreUnknownKeys = true`, so keys with no matching property are skipped

questions.explanation: By default, kotlinx.serialization fails when the JSON has a key the class doesn't declare. `ignoreUnknownKeys = true` skips such keys, which lets the server add fields without breaking old app versions. `coerceInputValues` only covers nulls for non-nullable properties and unknown enum values, and `isLenient` only relaxes quoting rules.

sources.title: Customize the Json instance
sources.claim: By default, unknown keys result in an error during deserialization unless `ignoreUnknownKeys = true`; `coerceInputValues` treats null for non-nullable types and unknown enum values as missing, so the default is used; `isLenient` only relaxes quoting rules; `encodeDefaults` affects encoding; `explicitNulls = false` omits null values.

questions.prompt: Users search 50,000 offline notes by word with `WHERE body LIKE '%' || :term || '%'`, and it's slow. How would you add full-text search with Room, and what would you watch out for?

model_answer.summary: Back the search with an FTS4 (or FTS5) virtual table queried with `MATCH`, ideally in external-content mode over the notes table so the text isn't stored twice, and pick a tokenizer that fits the language.
key_points: `LIKE '%term%'` is slow for word search; SQLite's own example shows an FTS `MATCH` query taking about 0.03 s where the `LIKE` query took 22.5 s
Add an `@Fts4` entity (an FTS virtual table) and search it with `MATCH`; if it declares a primary key, it must be an INTEGER column named `rowid`
Use `contentEntity = Note::class` so the FTS table doesn't duplicate the text; Room creates triggers to keep it in sync, so write only to the notes table (the triggers are dropped during migrations)
Choose a tokenizer, such as `porter`, which stems English words so 'frustrated' also matches 'frustration'

questions.explanation: An FTS table keeps an index of the words in each row, which is what makes word queries fast. External-content mode saves the space of a second copy of every note, at the cost of keeping the two tables in sync, which Room's triggers do for normal writes but not inside migrations.

sources.title: Define data using Room entities
sources.claim: For fast full-text search, back entities with an FTS virtual table using `@Fts3`, `@Fts4` or `@Fts5`; FTS tables always use an INTEGER primary key named `rowid`; the `tokenizer` option picks how text is tokenized.

sources.title: Fts4
sources.claim: With `contentEntity`, the FTS table works in external content mode and doesn't store its own content; Room creates triggers to keep the tables in sync, so all writes should go to the content entity table; the triggers are removed before migrations and re-created after.

sources.title: SQLite FTS3 and FTS4 Extensions
sources.claim: In SQLite's example, a MATCH query on an FTS table returned in about 0.03 s versus 22.5 s for LIKE '%linux%' on an ordinary table; the porter tokenizer stems words so 'Frustration' matches 'Frustrated'.

questions.prompt:
```kotlin
launch(Dispatchers.Default + tl.asContextElement("A")) {
  tl.set("B")
  delay(10)
  println(tl.get())
}
```
What does it print?

choices.text: B, because `set` copies the new value into the context element
B, as long as the coroutine resumes on the same thread as before
null, because a resumed coroutine starts with an empty value
A, because the change is lost at the next suspension point

questions.explanation: The context element restores the value it was created with every time the coroutine resumes. It can't track direct `ThreadLocal` writes, so a value set with `set` inside the coroutine is lost at the next suspension, whichever thread it resumes on. To change the value for a block, use `withContext(tl.asContextElement("B"))`.

sources.title: Coroutine context and dispatchers
sources.claim: `ThreadLocal.asContextElement` keeps a value and restores it every time the coroutine switches its context; a value set inside the coroutine is not propagated and is lost on the next suspension (use `withContext` to change it); `Dispatchers.Unconfined` resumes on whatever thread the suspending function used.

questions.prompt: A model has `val status: Status = Status.UNKNOWN`. The server starts sending `"status": "ARCHIVED"`, which the enum lacks, and decoding fails. Which `Json` setting makes it decode as `UNKNOWN`?

choices.text: `ignoreUnknownKeys = true`, which skips values the app doesn't know
`coerceInputValues = true`, which treats the unknown value as missing
`encodeDefaults = true`, which makes the decoder fall back to defaults
`isLenient = true`, which accepts any string for an enum property

questions.explanation: `coerceInputValues` treats certain invalid input as if the property were missing: a null for a non-nullable type, or an enum value the app doesn't know. A missing property gets its default, here `UNKNOWN`. `ignoreUnknownKeys` is about unknown keys, not values, and `encodeDefaults` only affects encoding.

sources.title: Customize the Json instance
sources.claim: By default, unknown keys result in an error during deserialization unless `ignoreUnknownKeys = true`; `coerceInputValues` treats null for non-nullable types and unknown enum values as missing, so the default is used; `isLenient` only relaxes quoting rules; `encodeDefaults` affects encoding; `explicitNulls = false` omits null values.

questions.prompt: You declare `@Fts4(contentEntity = Note::class)` on a `NoteFts` entity. Where should the app insert new notes?

choices.text: Into both tables in one transaction, so that the two stay consistent
Into `NoteFts` only, since Room copies its rows back to the notes table
Into `Note` only: Room's triggers keep `NoteFts` in sync with it
Into `Note`, then rebuild `NoteFts` by hand after each batch of writes

questions.explanation: With `contentEntity`, the FTS table runs in external-content mode: it stores no text of its own and reads it from the `Note` table. Room creates triggers that keep the two in sync, so all writes go to the content entity. The exception is a migration, when Room removes the triggers and you may need to write to both.
